blocks.text: A5 Inclusion fact base
The Inclusion Plan scores 107 long-listed communities down to a shortlist of 20, rates their readiness, sizes the spend they could capture and takes its order of action from five benchmark cases.
Long-list rule and scoring weights

The long-list takes every Census 2011 sub-place cluster with 1,500 people or more and official unemployment of 25% or more, plus named mission, fishing and farm settlements (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p14). The rule yields 107 township and rural communities with 2.81 million people in 2011 (48% of the province) and 3.79 million on the 2025 estimate (p16). Of the 107, 93 sit within 45 minutes of one of 35 supply-report nodes or three corridors (p16).

By region the long-list holds Cape Metro 26, Cape Winelands 16, Overberg 19, Garden Route 23, West Coast 13 and Central Karoo 10 (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p16). The shortlist takes five from Cape Metro and three from each other region (p16). Need rests on Census 2011 because Census 2022 is not published below municipality and ward and asked no income question (p15).

blocks.message: Need carries the largest weight of the five criteria, and each criterion scores a community from 3 to 1 against printed thresholds.

blocks.text: Archetypes and responses

Two tests set the archetype: a 45-minute drive time to the nearest node or corridor and whether any attraction sits inside the boundary (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p4, p14). Atlantis is held remote by Wesgro naming at 26 minutes from Darling (p17). For the largest group the plan's diagnosis is that "the product and the node's demand are there; the seller is missing" (p15).

blocks.message: Proximate communities with underused assets are the largest group on both lists, and the plan pairs each archetype with a response, a first move and a benchmark.

blocks.text: The counts give 92 proximate communities against 93 within 45 minutes on p16 (computed). Doringbaai and Laingsburg (Bergsig) carry different archetypes on their profiles than on the shortlist (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p18, p25, p26). Knysna northern townships and Kwa-Mandlenkosi are scored as having no community-based product but "assets underused on the evidence" (p56, p58).
Readiness of the shortlisted communities

The plan rates each shortlisted community Ready, Developing or Gap from the community side, with LTO confirmation outstanding (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p27, p28). Digital and bookability comes from the 19 profile pages; Gugulethu has no profile (p20 to p26, p40 to p51).

blocks.caption: Shortlist readiness ratings
blocks.source: SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026: p53 to p58 for the binding constraint; p28 for organisation present, benefit visible to residents and assets protected or damaged; p27 for safety perception; p20 to p26 and p40 to p51 for digital and bookability. Rows follow the shortlist order on p18; section 2.6 prints each community's archetype, score and drive time. Counts are tallied from the printed cells (computed).
blocks.message: Half the shortlist has no identified active tourism body, and no community is rated Ready on benefit visible to residents or on digital and bookability.

blocks.text: The remaining ratings are counted in the order Ready, Developing and Gap. On p27, extortion is 10, 5, 5; energy supply 6, 14, 0; water and sanitation 1, 14, 5; coach access 0, 20, 0; service delivery 1, 14, 5 (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p27, computed). In the 19 profiles, air and road access is 2, 16, 1; accommodation range 0, 5, 14; safety and support 0, 11, 8 (p20 to p26, p40 to p51, computed).

Extortion is a Gap in Khayelitsha, Atlantis, Mitchells Plain, Gugulethu and Kayamandi (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p27). Binding constraints tally Organisation 11, Attraction 6, Safety 1, Market link 1 and Infrastructure 1 (p53 to p58). The p28 headline counts six communities with asset damage against five Gap cells. The plan names no pilot community and assigns no owner; it tests two to three of six profiled exemplars and lists stakeholders for validation only (p32, p53 to p58).
Spend capture scenarios

The 20 communities hold 18.4% of Western Cape residents but a documented floor of R4m to R10m a year in visitor spend, while 1% of FY2025 foreign direct spend would land R259m (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p5; values as printed, with no tracing method or denominator printed). They also hold 15.4% of employed residents; both shares come from Census 2011. Foreign direct spend traced to businesses trading inside the communities is a floor of 0.02% to 0.04%, which the plan documents as R4m to R10m landing in the 20 communities a year.

At 1%, FY2025 foreign direct spend would land R259m in the communities, which implies R25.9 billion of FY2025 foreign direct spend (computed). At 1% of the 2035 spend ambition the figure is R547m, which implies R54.7 billion of spend in 2035 (computed). The plan cites the Demand-Side Analysis (16 Sep 2026) and Diagnostic Report v2 for that scenario (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p5). The Diagnostic sets the ambition as 5.7 million international arrivals and R54.7 billion of tourism spend by 2035 (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p5), a different case from the 2.5 million this report carries. Appendix A2 sets out the demand model's own 2035 cases.
Benchmark cases and the order of action

The five cases point to one order of action: "a seller with a stake, a safe and workable visit, product that keeps spend in the community, then exposure" (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p12). The plan's six takeaways are that a sustainable local operator is essential, resident ownership matters, safety is a prerequisite, local spend should be captured, existing product should be sold and spending should be tracked (p12).

The plan finds that local selling mechanisms lasted while assets and training without a durable route to market did not, but Costa Rica's selling network did not survive donor exit (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p7 to p12, p30; the Rio, Medellín, Vilakazi Street and Kliptown cards print no source line, and the plan pools their sources on p12).

**Rio de Janeiro, Santa Marta and Rocinha.** The Rio Top Tour's first phase cost about R$230,000 (R$184,000 federal, R$46,000 state). The Cantagalo elevator cost about R$89 million and the Providência cable car R$75 million in a R$163 million package, and almost 10,000 officers were deployed at peak (p7). The tours drew about 4,500 visitors in their first month in 2010, and about 20 resident guides were working by 2015. In 2014, 81% of foreign visitors spent up to R$10 in Rocinha. The cable car stood idle for eight years and security collapsed in 2017, yet Rocinha drew 544,000 visitors in 2023. Access and safety were preconditions, not product, and resident guides continued after the programme that launched them (p30).

**Medellín, Comuna 13.** Metrocable Line J (2008) cost about 96.9 billion pesos and the escalators (2011) about 10 billion pesos, with maintenance above 260 million pesos a year; the integrated urban programme passed 100 billion pesos by 2020 (p8). Comuna 13 drew 1.66 million visitors in 2022 and 1.98 million in 2025, 52% of them international, with more than 1,000 businesses and about 300 guides. A 2023 study put its capacity at 667 visitors a day. The lesson is to fund a mandate, a capacity ceiling and a community body alongside the escalator; residents developed the product first (p30).

**Soweto, Vilakazi Street.** The Hector Pieterson Museum cost R23.2 million, the Mandela House restoration about R9 million from corporate donors and Orlando Stadium about R280 million; the public-realm cost is not disclosed (p9). The street drew about 1,000 tourists a day by January 2010. Sakhumzi grew from four employees in 2001 to about 110 in 2019, and the ten restaurants provide more than 800 jobs, though the Mandela House company was liquidated. Upgrades amplified existing assets but benefits concentrated on street-front owners, so design governance and a resident precinct entity belong at the outset.

**Costa Rica, ACTUAR.** UNDP GEF small grants funded the network from the 1990s. Law 8724 (2009) gave ICT duties without a budget, and no state funding for the selling network has been identified (p10). ACTUAR, founded in 2001, turned over more than USD 800,000 in 2013 for more than 30 member communities and dissolved at the end of 2018; its benefits "stopped at association members". A management entity with its own selling channel was the engine, and it did not survive donor exit.

**Soweto, Kliptown.** Kliptown received R436 million in its first allocation. The JDA spent about R497 million from 2001 to 2010 plus R40 million to 2013, Walter Sisulu Square cost R160 million to R180 million and a 48-room hotel R24 million (p11). The business case projected almost 200,000 international visitors a year, but the museum drew about 4,000 a year by 2017 and the hotel traded above break-even only during the 2010 FIFA World Cup. Local small businesses took 5% of construction contract value, and the site was looted in 2021. Heritage converts to local income only when operator, trader and guide product, security and services are funded before the ribbon is cut.
